title: The sower (Matthew 13:1–9)
hook: seed lands on path, rock, thorns and good soil; most is wasted, and the harvest is huge anyway
tomorrow: The mustard seed and the yeast (Matthew 13:31–33)

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was parable, and your line was a story carries what a lecture can't. Did you tell anyone a story instead of making a point? Today, the first real one. Day twenty-three.

A farmer walks the edge of his field with a bag of seed on his hip. He reaches in, takes a handful, and flings it in a wide arc. Then another. He isn't placing seeds one by one. He's throwing. Some lands on the hard footpath, and the birds have it before he's finished the row. Some lands where the rock is just under a skin of soil. It shoots up fast, and the first hot day kills it. Some lands among thorns and gets strangled. And some lands in good ground. That's the whole story. Jesus told it sitting in a boat, to a crowd on the shore, and plenty of them had done exactly this with their own hands. They knew how much seed a farmer loses. What they didn't expect was the ending.
screen: `A FARMER THROWING SEED.` → `PATH, ROCK, THORNS, GOOD GROUND.` → `THEY DIDN'T EXPECT THE ENDING.`

segments.voice: It starts: "Behold, a sower went forth to sow." Look how much goes wrong. Three kinds of ground out of four fail. If you were keeping count, you'd call this a story about waste. Then the last line. The good ground "brought forth fruit, some an hundredfold, some sixtyfold, some thirtyfold." Many scholars think an ordinary good harvest then was far smaller than that. A hundredfold is the kind of number that makes a farmer laugh out loud. So the surprise isn't the failure. Everyone knew about failure. The surprise is that the harvest dwarfs it. A little further on in the same chapter, the Gospel gives an explanation, told to the disciples. The seed is the word, the good news of God's kingdom. The kinds of ground are kinds of listeners: the one who hears and loses it at once, the one who's thrilled for a week, the one whose worries choke it, the one who lets it grow. Christians have heard the story from two sides, and often both at once. Some hear it about the sower: keep throwing, even when most of it seems wasted, because you can't see where the good ground is. Some hear it about the soil: what kind of ground am I, today? And notice something. The farmer doesn't test the soil first. He doesn't save his seed for the good patch. He throws it everywhere, on the path and the rock and the thorns, as if there's plenty to go around. It ends: "Who hath ears to hear, let him hear." The story stops, and hands the question to the listener.
screen: `A SOWER WENT FORTH TO SOW` · `THREE GROUNDS OUT OF FOUR FAIL` · `A HUNDREDFOLD` · `THE SOWER, OR THE SOIL?` · then, large: `HE THROWS IT EVERYWHERE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Two minutes. Sit and let your breathing slow down. Now picture the four kinds of ground: the hard path, the thin soil over rock, the thorns, the good earth. Don't grade yourself. Just notice. Which one are you today? Maybe the path, too trampled to take anything in. Maybe the thorns: plenty of life, but the worries are winning. Maybe good ground, open and ready. Whatever it is, it's only today. Ground changes. Paths get broken up. Thorns get pulled. Breathe, and let yourself be whatever ground you are. The bell holds the time.
The sower. A farmer throwing seed everywhere, as if there's plenty, and a harvest that dwarfs the waste. Today's story on your strand.
Your line: keep throwing seed. Today, do one good thing without checking first whether it'll land. A kind word. An offer of help. Throw it. Day twenty-three.

screen: `DAY 23 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE MUSTARD SEED AND THE YEAST.`

howItsDone: The parable of the sower is one of the best known in churches, read in the Gospel of Matthew, Mark or Luke; many Christians hear it as a question about how they receive the word, and as encouragement to keep sharing it.

fork.setup: you're a farmer with a bag of seed. you can see the path, the rocks and the thorns. what do you do?
options: throw it everywhere, on all of it.
fork.reveal: the sower in the story throws everywhere, on path, rock and thorns. most of it is lost, and the harvest is still a hundredfold.

original.note: Greek: "the one sowing," from speirō, to scatter seed. English spore and diaspora come from the same family.

trapdoor: what you thought: a story about good people and bad people.
what it means: a story about a generous sower, and a harvest bigger than all the waste.
what a scholar hears: many scholars think an ordinary good yield was far below a hundredfold, so the ending is meant to astonish. Matthew 13:18–23 adds the explanation.

notes: Ancient grain yields: the script says only that 'many scholars think' an ordinary good harvest was far smaller than a hundredfold. Estimates vary (often given as around tenfold); confirm the wording.
The parable also appears in Mark 4 and Luke 8; the script follows Matthew's wording.
